catalog_quote: Mauritian Creole is a stress-timed language. Three kinds of syllable can be identified: (1) Unstressable in all circumstances: These include the TAM markers (§6), subject personal pronouns (§5.1) and possessive adjectives, the articles en and la, the final syllable of long forms of verbs with both short and long forms, most prepositions, etc. (2) Obligatorily stressed in all circumstances: These include the prefixes ré- and dé-, the emphasizer mém, the number én ‘one’ etc. (3) Stressable: All nouns, adjectives, verbs, and adverbs contain at least one stressable syllable which may be pronounced without stress when adjacent to another word containing a stressed syllable, depending on the rhythm of delivery adopted by the speaker. Note that stress placement can distinguish between two different words or meanings which would otherwise be represented graphically as identical, e.g. refér ‘to …
sweep_summary: Three title hits for mori1278; none changes the catalog. Two (Goad & White 2004 EUROSLA Yearbook; Goad & White 2006 Second Language Research) are Glottolog misattachments: L2-English inflection studies of a Turkish L1 speaker (confirmed from the Benjamins first-page preview, saved) and of 10 Mandarin L1 speakers (Crossref abstract); both paywalled, no Morisyen content, priority none. The third, Mamode 2015 (CLA proceedings), is open and fetched sources : it is about Mauritian French, not the creole; on Mauritian Creole it only relays phrase-level findings from Mamode 2014 (UWO MA mémoire, AP-initial accentuation, AP/IP-final H tone and final lengthening) and says nothing about word-stress placement; the 2014 mémoire itself was not findable in Western's Scholaris repository or CORE (medium priority to acquire). Best first-hand statement read this sweep remains Baker & Kriegel 2013 §4.3 p. 253 (already the catalog's deciding source; supports the 'lexical' coding); Martin 1995 on file shows word-final perceived stress in read sentences but no rule. Receipts: written at with md5s and fetch stamps. discovery went to automated fetch (CLA index, Crossref, OpenAlex, CORE, Scholaris REST).

Three kinds of syllable can be identified: (1) Unstressable in all circumstances: these include the TAM markers (§6), subject personal pronouns (§5.1) and possessive adjectives, the articles en and la, the final syllable of long forms of verbs with both short and long forms, most prepositions, etc. (2) Obligatorily stressed in all circumstances: these include the prefixes ré- and dé-, the emphasizer mém, the number én 'one', etc. (3) Stressable: all nouns, adjectives, verbs, and adverbs contain at least one stressable syllable [...] Note that stress placement can distinguish two different words or meanings [...] refér 'to recover (from an ailment)' versus réfer 'to make or do again'
new_statements.citation: Baker, Philip & Sibylle Kriegel. 2013. Mauritian Creole. In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath & Huber (eds.), The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages, vol. II, 250-260. Oxford: OUP. (HAL hal-01481685 author copy)
new_statements.reading: Stress is specified per morpheme/syllable class (unstressable, obligatorily stressed, stressable) and its placement is contrastive (refér vs réfer, la vs lá, kúd-kúd vs kud-kúd); no positional default is stated, and stressable syllables lose stress rhythmically next to a stressed word. This is the same passage and source the catalog already relies on, and it supports the catalog's 'lexical' coding. The only other first-hand prosodic data on file, Martin 1995 (ICPhS, pp. 644-647, read this sweep), marks every perceived stressed vowel in read sentences on the word-final syllable, a phrase-level final-prominence tendency, but states no word-stress rule. Nothing found in this sweep supersedes Baker & Kriegel.

sources.note: Per Mamode 2015 §3.3 it is an acoustic sketch of Mauritian Creole declarative prosody (AP-initial accentuation, AP/IP-final H tone, final syllables up to ~300 ms). Unknown whether it states a word-stress rule; the only instrumental prosody study of the creole besides Martin 1995, so worth locating (UWO French Studies MA; may never have been deposited).

sources.note: The only dedicated phonetics/phonology monograph on Mauritian Creole (named in the 2025 état de l'art as one of eight phonology publications); our LEXICAL coding is inferred from per-word acute marking in an 11-page sketch that states no positional rule, and a monograph-length treatment is the most likely place for an explicit word-stress rule or default.
